title: Flesh, breath, ruling part
hookLine: you're flesh, breath and a ruling mind; don't let the mind be a slave (Meditations 2.2)
tomorrow: Throw away the thirst for books

cards: Book one was thanks. Book two, perhaps begun in camp, opens differently.
After a first entry about the difficult people he'll meet today, read on this path before, Marcus turns to himself and does something like a doctor's exam.
He takes himself apart into three pieces, names each one, and asks which of them is in charge. The first is the plainest: flesh.

teach.h: A LITTLE FLESH, BREATH, RULING PART.

teach.b: Section two opens, in Long's translation: "Whatever this is that I am, it is a little flesh and breath, and the ruling part." Notice the humility of whatever this is.
The emperor of Rome isn't sure what he is, and he's starting from the ground up. Second, flesh. He's blunt here: as if you were already dying, he tells himself, look down on the flesh.
Then he looks at it like an anatomy student: blood, bones, a woven net of nerves, veins and arteries. He doesn't call the body evil. He's refusing to let it be the thing that runs his life.
Third, breath. What is it? Air, and not even the same air from one moment to the next, breathed out and drawn in, again and again.
You've been watching it on this path for hundreds of days; Marcus noticed it too, perhaps in a tent.

teach.h: THE RULING PART HOLDS THE STRINGS.
teach.b: Fourth, the ruling part, the mind that judges and chooses. The Stoics called it the hegemonikon, the part that leads. And here Marcus gives himself an order.
You're no longer young, he says.
Don't let this part be a slave any longer, pulled by strings like a puppet, jerked into selfish moves. Don't let it grumble at the present or shrink from the future. That's the picture to carry.
The flesh pulls. The appetites pull. Other people's opinions pull.
Everyone has strings. The question is whether the ruling part is holding them, or hanging from them.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism do Marcus's three-part check (body, breath, mind) during the day, asking whether their mind is choosing or being pulled.

o: the strongest of the three parts, meant to lead
a Greek word for the mind that judges and chooses
the body, first of Marcus's three parts of a person

games.q: flesh, breath, ruling part — tap the pairs.
p: blood, bones, a net of nerves

s: Marcus says the body is evil
he tells himself to look down on the flesh, as if dying, but he never calls it evil.
Marcus opens with 'whatever this is that I am'
"Whatever this is that I am, it is a little flesh and breath, and the ruling part."
the ruling part is the breath
it's the third part: the mind that judges and chooses.

games.q: a message lands, and you feel the familiar jerk: reply now, angrily. you're Marcus's ruling part. what do you do?
o: follow the pull; that's how you feel.
notice the string, and decide for yourself.
throw the phone across the room.
games.why: Marcus tells the ruling part not to be pulled by the strings like a puppet. noticing the string is the first move.

practice: Do Marcus's exam: feel your weight in the chair, then watch the air go out and come in, never quite the same air twice, then notice the thing that's noticing.
Ask it, gently, what's been pulling your strings today, a worry, a craving, a message, someone's opinion, and name one string.

wordCard.voice: Flesh. The first of Marcus's three parts: a little flesh, breath, and the ruling mind, which shouldn't be pulled by strings like a puppet. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the ruling part, the Stoic name for the mind that judges and chooses.

carryVoice: Your line: not a puppet. A little flesh, a little breath, and a mind that leads. See you tomorrow.
